item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I have never enjoyed skips/tales that give an inevitable end-of-the-world scenario that the Foundation cannot avoid. It's the implication of such a situation that tends to turn me off 231, far more than Procedure 110-Montauk. For me at least unstoppable doom inspires more apathy than horror. If there's nothing to be done why should I care? If, however, there is something that can be done but we might fail to do it, that's actually interesting to me.
I mention all this to note why I love this tale. 999 isn't guaranteed to save the day and defeat the Scarlet King. But it might. And that as a setup stimulates my imagination far more than either in isolation.
Even Lovecraft let the humans win from time to time.

item.title: Re: Not dark enough
item.content:encoded:
Although keeping your humanity is important, and they did do some horrible things to that child, I'd say that an organization that almost decided to carry out 110-Montauk for an extended period of time would consider it worthy to keep her under lockdown with the fate of the Multiverse at stake.

SCP-231 makes it clear that whatever Procedure 110-Montauk is it's so utterly horrible that the Foundation staff working on it won't even admit to others within the Foundation what they're doing and those on the project have to have their memories removed afterwards just to maintain their sanity. And this is the same organisation that casually sends off human beings to vile deaths or worse just for the sake of testing in every other article and is quite happy to say as much, even celebrate the results. It seems reasonable to me that under those circumstances their guilt might outweigh their ruthless practicality, particularly since it's 999 remaining secret that really matters, not his mother.

it completely deviates from the original SCP's dark, hopeless tone.

Except that's rather the point. This story is meant to be a hopeful conclusion to 231's very dark story. It is, of course, entirely fair to dislike that idea in concept but it seems odd to criticise the story for doing exactly what it set out to do.

item.title: Not dark enough
item.content:encoded:
I like your storytelling and the idea that Procedure 110-Montauk is too suspiciously convenient and thus fake. I'd wonder why the Children of the Scarlet King would make the procedure so complex (since it was bound to fail, and then the Foundation would realize it was fake), but that could be explained by the Scarlet King being summoned by the ritual before the Foundation found out.

However, it doesn't seem like the Foundation to just release the girl back and do all that stuff for "compensation". The C in SCP doesn't stand for Compensate. If word got out that 231-7 was still alive, who knows what would happen? So why would they release her and her entire family back into a town where they could be discovered again, and even give her a large sum of money to attract attention with?

Sure, the Foundation would most likely have them under heavy surveillance. But wouldn't it be much safer to keep them on base far away from prying eyes? Although keeping your humanity is important, and they did do some horrible things to that child, I'd say that an organization that almost decided to carry out 110-Montauk for an extended period of time would consider it worthy to keep her under lockdown with the fate of the Multiverse at stake.

I respect your attempt to link SCP-999 to the Scarlet King, and you gave an admirable theory on how he could 'defeat' the Scarlet King. But needless to say there's too many plot holes to have this stand up to even basic scrutiny and it completely deviates from the original SCP's dark, hopeless tone.

Maybe [most likely] I'm complaining too much since this is, in fact, a tale made by someone other than the author, and there is, of course, no real canon. I'm not going to downvote this, but still, I can't help but question its premise.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Wow, 12 comments in 5 hours on an 18-month-old tale.

Well Baronjoe, regarding the logic of this tale, you need to keep in mind that the Brides are also Eldritch Horrors. They are his daughters/sisters, and are the same type of Old God as the Scarlet King, and as such they have the same sort of abilities as him and he is not able to flawlessly prevent them from exercising these abilities against him. Quote: "Her children walked on two legs, and were mighty hunters and heroes: she taught them in secret, hoping that they might destroy the children of her sisters and overthrow the King. They are few, and they have failed."

The Seventh Bride intentionally made her children to fight their father and kept them a secret. The Scarlet King, like Kronos, fears being overthrown by his son because he is not all-powerful, and just like Zeus was successfully kept hidden until he was strong enough to challenge his father, so too is SCP-999.

I'm really surprised so many other authors came to the defense of this tale, and I agree with their responses so I won't repeat them.

Baronjoe, I disagree with you when you say that Light and Dark cannot coexist (I would actually go so far as to say one cannot exist without the other) and one must destroy the other, and I agree with Fieldstone when he says that love and forgiveness are more effective at resolving conflicts than fighting. We can't beat the Scarlet King through sheer force, so we need to try another tactic.

I make no claims that this tale is perfect, but I do not apologize for its lack of grimdarkness. I write silly tales about a magic circus because there's a niche for that here, because some readers need a break from the grimdark. Some people love the grimdarkness of SCP-230, but as Theesherm pointed out in his recent reading of it, some people really do need it to have a happy ending, and I am honoured that this tale was one of the happy endings he recommended.

Have a disquieting day.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Funny, I dislike the premise of 999, but find this to be the perfect narrative use of it.

+ on the nature of evil
– hide block

I get where you're coming from about love and evil, but have to disagree. Having spent the last decade as a social services therapist, I've routinely confronted unspeakably ugly situations and the people who created them, and intensively studied how people change and the ways that punishment and suffering affect them. I can assure you that love (channeled effectively) is the only way to redeem the vast majority of what we describe as evil.

Meeting anger and fear with more of the same is simply ineffective. Trust and believe that if it worked, we would do it - there are some dark chapters in the history of behavior science where that approach has been tried. Rising above the urge to hurt whatever is hurting you is a necessary first step to realistically solving problems in any relationship; the whole point of the Scarlet King is that it's too powerful for the Foundation to just outfight, so this provides an alternative in removing the enemy's desire to cause harm in the first place. That's actually a pretty powerful allegory for the problems of addressing real-world violence.

Eldritch god love is different from human love, just like their evil is different from our evil, but that's what mythological beings are - scaled up versions of things around us, that allow us to see the familiar from a new perspective.

item.content:encoded:
The quality of the writing is decent but I hate the interpretation. SCP-999 is just this thing that exists and I hate to imagine it being related to the Scarlet King because how? How does that work? It's like when a white guy ends up with a black son at birth. How does that work here? The evil dark Scarlet King spawns something so opposite is ridiculous and that slight self-awareness doesn't help. Honestly, it comes off as- and I hate using the word- cringey fanfiction. Especially incorporating 682 as its sibling since honestly I disagree with those two even being related, not less through the Scarlet King.

I’m sure you’re skeptical. Are we insane? How could our sweet little tickle monster ever hope to dethrone a Lovecraftian Horror of unparalleled might? Well, SCP-999 is less than a decade old. It’s still just a child, and nowhere near its full strength. Even so, its power is incredible. Even brief interaction with SCP-999 can permanently cure severe depression and PTSD, and more recent experiments have resulted in the complete reformation of D-class personnel who were previously unrepentant sociopaths. This effect is not chemical, but psychic, and one day it may grow powerful enough that not even the Scarlet King himself will be immune.

It will not overthrow the Scarlet King by force, but with light and love and laughter that can brighten the blackest of hearts.

This leans on Mary Sue levels. I don't have much of an issue with the premise of 999 but it should have limitations since it's just ridiculous to imagine it "over powering" an eldritch horror psychologically. So yeah, the "It's not even my final form" is a bit too ridiculous. Not to mention that how it's expected to end is childish overall.

The only redeemable quality is the thought of their being a connection with Sarkicism which gave me a new headcanon of their maybe being a relation since I imagine all gods are related in a way but I digress.

Overall, this article is childish and a lame fanfiction of 999 that fails at suspension of disbelief.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Agreeing with sirpudding above, and also adding the following:

While in some ways the commitment to the more outdated aspects of these articles is admirable (in that the dopey crosstests are canon, for example), the piece doesn't really click when those more campy aspects of these works are brought into direct comparison with newer material, such as with comparisons to Sarkicism and perhaps most subtly with the tone of the whole thing leaning towards that of the subversive Fear Alone.

The problem then is that it doesn't click together, and the whole piece doesn't cohere so much as the disparate elements just exist next to each other. This is exacerbated by the casual infodump tone, as it's difficult to actually subvert the audience's expectations when they're not really sure what they're supposed to be expecting.

The final effect is that it doesn't read as a serious and interesting subversion, it reads like someone describing their crazy fan theory at the water cooler. There's also this patronizing way that the piece walks the reader through every step in the logic, even taking the time to put every every possible plot notion to rest. For example, the entire paragraph about how the traumatized little girl is totally fine now seems incredibly dismissive, like you didn't want to address anything dark in the story… which isn't really possible given the darkness of 231's subject matter.

The characters (or character, should I say) reach this interesting point, the uncanny valley of genre-savviness in that they're so aware of being characters that they cease to be characters and just become conduits for the writer to disperse wit. This O5 sits squarely in that valley, constantly going through motions of "predicting" what the reader is thinking (and doing the aforementioned "walk the reader through everything") and as a result feeling incredibly plastic.

So, unfortunately, this story takes a promising premise but fumbles on the execution. There isn't a narrative so much as there's a walkthrough of events and convenient steps, and there aren't characters so much as there's a narrator who spends all his time winking at you. This leads to the whole tale not feeling like an exploration of an idea, just the idea stated to the reader as clearly and unambiguously as possible.

Summary: Downvote. Could fare significantly better with a serious rewrite, keeping most of the story intact.
